title: Praise, then ask
hookLine: the Fatiha praises for four verses before it asks for anything (1:1–7)

lines: OR: HELLO, THANK YOU, THEN THE ASK.
cards: A text arrives: can you lend me fifty dollars. No hello. No how are you.

Just the ask. Nothing wrong with it, exactly, but it lands hard. Now a different text: I was thinking about you this morning, you were so good to me last month, and, I hate to ask, could you help me out.
Same request. Different weight. The Fatiha is seven verses long, and for the first four of them it asks for nothing at all.

teach.h: FOUR VERSES ABOUT WHO GOD IS
teach.b: Count the verses as day three hundred thirty-three did, with the bismillah first. One: in the name of Allah, the Beneficent, the Merciful. Two: praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds.
Three: the Beneficent, the Merciful. Four: Owner of the Day of Judgment. Four verses, every one of them about who God is.
Then verse five turns: Thee alone we worship, Thee alone we ask for help. Only in verses six and seven comes a request: show us the straight path. A hadith makes that order explicit.

Fadalah ibn Ubayd reported, in the collections of Abu Dawud and at-Tirmidhi, that the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ heard a man making a supplication in his prayer without praising God or sending blessings on the Prophet.
He said: this man has rushed.
Then he taught: when one of you prays, begin with the praise of your Lord, then send blessings on the Prophet, then ask for whatever you wish.
So Muslim supplications are often taught in that shape: praise, blessing, then the need. Praise puts the one being addressed first, before the want. It also changes the asking.

A request made after four verses about mercy, lordship and judgment comes out smaller and clearer. The straight path, in the Fatiha, isn't a demand. It's what you ask for after you've remembered whom you're asking.

how: Many Muslims open a du'a by praising Allah and sending blessings on the Prophet before making their request, following the order of al-Fatiha and the hadith of Fadalah ibn Ubayd.

o: a song sung aloud at the end of the prayer
a polite word said to the imam after the prayer
honoring God for who He is, before any request

games.q: the order of a prayer — tap the pairs.

s: the Fatiha opens with a request for guidance
it praises for four verses first; the request comes in verses six and seven.
the Prophet taught: praise your Lord, send blessings on the Prophet, then ask
the hadith of Fadalah ibn Ubayd, in Abu Dawud and at-Tirmidhi.

games.q: a man in the mosque prays, and goes straight to what he needs. the Prophet hears him. what does he say?
o: this man's prayer is not accepted.
nothing; a request is a request.
games.why: he rushed. the Prophet doesn't reject the prayer; he teaches the order: praise, blessing on the Prophet, then ask for whatever you wish.

practice: Think of one thing you want, something real, large or small, and hold it without saying it yet. First, for a few breaths, name what you're grateful for, or, if you pray, what you know of God: merciful, near, the Lord of the worlds.
Then let the request come, and hear whether it sounds different when it finally arrives.

wordCard.voice: Praise. The Fatiha spends four verses on who God is before it asks for anything, and the hadith calls skipping that step rushing. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: extolling, speaking well of someone; often used for the praise that opens a du'a.

carryVoice: Your line: praise first. The asking can wait four verses. That's day three hundred thirty-five.

sources.q: Owner of the Day of Judgment

sources.ref: Sunan Abi Dawud 1481; Jami' at-Tirmidhi 3477 (hadith of Fadalah ibn Ubayd: this man has rushed)
